poems:
11:00 p.m. exactly.
Somewhere a meeting is being scheduled
for a time you will be asleep.

11:01. Contact lenses out.
The room goes soft at the edges.

He says he is going to bed.
He says it from the couch.
Freight train through Lynchburg, two towns of people rolling over without waking.
Tomorrow's outfit laid across the chair like a person who gave up.

Set the alarm.
Set the second alarm.
Do not calculate the hours remaining.
You will calculate them anyway.
A dog gets up, turns twice, lies down facing the door.
The hallway smoke detector chirps once and waits eleven months.
The ice maker drops its load. Somebody upstairs decides it was nothing.

11:09 p.m.
The text says no worries.
It took nine minutes to write.
Retainer in. Conversation over.
The couple's ten minutes ran long, which is the best thing that happened today.
One porch bulb on Ridge Street, for nobody, on a timer since 2009.

11:13 p.m. The chip bag clipped shut
with the good clip, a small ceremony.
11:14 p.m. Your phone offers a summary of your day. Decline.
Quarter past. The night shift signs in, and somebody has taken the good chair.
Rain or no rain, the gutter on the north side has an opinion.
Two teenagers, one house, three feet apart, texting each other about a third.

Receipt, 11:18 p.m.
TALL DRIP  2.85
CASH
NO REFUNDS
The last dish set to drain at an angle no engineer would approve.

Somebody's mother is still awake
in a time zone she keeps for him.
The laundry got folded. The laundry did not get put away. The laundry is a tomorrow problem, and tomorrow has been notified.
Streetlamp, moth, the same argument as last night.

11:23 p.m.
The phone is put on the nightstand
like a lid being put on something.
In the ER waiting room, a man holds a coat that is not his size.
Tomorrow, n., a storage facility.

11:26 p.m. One cabinet door left open,
confessing nothing.
The bar on the next block empties in the wrong order: the loud ones first, then the ones who came to talk.
Toothbrush timer. Two minutes. An eternity.
The baby monitor shows a gray room and one small back rising.
Half past eleven, the half hour that still thinks it is early.

Somewhere a bakery's first mixer is already turning,
three alarms from now.

Stove.
Door.
The thing you forgot.
Door again.
Ceiling fan on low, pull chain ticking against the globe.
The day's argument comes back with better lines. Too late. Excellent lines.

11:35 p.m. A siren far off, rising, falling,
somebody else's story.

11:36 p.m. Six hours and twenty-four minutes,
if you go now.
Noted.
The cat has business.
Charger cable found by feel, plugged in on the fourth attempt, victory declared.
Blue glow on a face on a pillow. Twelve minutes ago this was going to be five minutes.
Hospital corridor, a cart with one bad wheel, arriving from a long way off.
Overheard through the wall: that is not what I said. Then nothing. Then a faucet.
The plant nobody waters is doing fine.
Under the door, a strip of hallway.

11:44 p.m. The grocery list gains an item
it will lose by the store.
Bar back stacking stools upside down, four to a table, the geometry of closing.
You said one more episode at 10:15.
The pill organizer, one compartment open, whichever day it is.

11:48 p.m. In Tokyo it is lunchtime.
Someone is having the fish, happily.
A porch chair, empty, still rocking a little.
Ten to midnight. The hour puts on its coat and looks for its keys.
Tomorrow rehearsed in full, for an audience of one, who has notes.
Somewhere a lock turns twice because once was not convincing.
11:53 p.m. The hamper accepts its last argument.
11:54 p.m. The night nurse writes the time in a box, which makes it official.
Five minutes of day left and it is spending them on a video about a lathe.
A glass of water set down where the hand will find it.

Phone face down.
Phone face up.
Phone face down.
The last honest thought of the day arrives, brief, unrepeatable, filed under tomorrow.
11:59 p.m. Nothing changes at the turn. Everybody acts like it does, and everybody is a little bit right.
